opus-5.5.text:
I think simplicity matters because of how scaling actually works. When you set a pretraining objective, you're defining what the model will spend trillions of tokens getting better at. Next-token prediction looks almost naive, but it's general. To predict the next token well across code, math, dialogue, and literature, the model has to build internal representations of a huge amount of structure in the world. The objective doesn't need to say "learn reasoning" or "learn facts." Those come out of it.

When people add complicated auxiliary losses or very hand-designed objectives, they're often putting their own assumptions about what intelligence should look like into the training signal. At small scale that can help, and you get nice gains on a benchmark. But as you scale data and compute, those assumptions tend to become constraints. The model would have found a better solution on its own, and you've pushed it toward yours. Many clever tricks that look good in a paper simply disappear, or even hurt, once you go up an order of magnitude.

Architecture is similar. A simple, uniform architecture is much easier to scale, debug, and optimize at the systems level. When you're training on thousands of GPUs, every unusual component costs you something in communication, memory, and stability. If something goes wrong in a very complex design, it's hard to tell whether the problem is the idea, the implementation, or the interaction between ten different modules. With a simple design, you can reason about it and iterate quickly.

That doesn't mean we never innovate on architecture. Things like mixture-of-experts or more efficient attention matter a lot. But the good innovations usually make the system *more* efficient while keeping the core clean. They remove a bottleneck rather than add a new mechanism. The question I ask is whether a change will still matter when the model is ten times bigger, or whether it only matters now because the model is small.

So the philosophy is to keep the foundation simple and general, and let scale and data do the heavy lifting. Then put your creativity where it really pays off: data quality, training efficiency, infrastructure, and later in post-training, where you're shaping how the model uses what it has already learned.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how scale can make hand-designed training objectives restrictive and says post-training shapes model behavior, but it does not say that prolonged post-training may invalidate constraints imposed by architecture design goals.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to what you're actually optimizing for. The goal of pretraining is to compress as much of the world as possible into the model. So the objective should be the one that keeps getting better as you scale compute and data, and that's really just next-token prediction. Every time people have tried to add clever auxiliary objectives or hand-designed inductive biases, those tricks tend to help at small scale and then get washed out, or even hurt, once you scale up. The simple objective is the one with the cleanest scaling law.

Same thing with architecture. If you make it complicated, you have more knobs, and every knob is a place where you might be baking in an assumption that's wrong. A simple architecture lets the data decide. It also matters a lot for engineering. When you're training on thousands of GPUs, every unusual component is something that has to be made efficient, made numerically stable, made to work with your parallelism strategy. Simplicity is what lets you actually run the experiments and trust the results.

And there's a research reason too. If the system is simple, then when something improves, you can tell why. You can isolate the variable. With a complicated system, you often get improvements and you can't tell whether it was the new attention variant or the data or just noise. So I'd say: keep the objective simple, keep the architecture simple, and put the effort into data quality, infrastructure, and scaling. That's where the real leverage is.

r001.rationale: The response argues for simple architectures but does not mention prolonged post-training or the risk that it may invalidate constraints imposed by architectural design goals.

astra-6.text:
I think the goal should be simple because we want the model to learn from the data, rather than force it to follow too many assumptions we’ve built into the system. With pretraining, a simple objective can still require very complex capabilities. Predicting the next token, for example, can involve understanding context, knowledge, and reasoning.

For architecture, simplicity also makes it easier to scale and to understand what’s actually working. Every extra component introduces interactions and makes experiments harder to interpret. That doesn’t mean we should never add complexity, but it should solve a clear problem and show a clear benefit. The complexity of the model’s behavior doesn’t have to come from complexity in its design.

r001.rationale: The response discusses keeping objectives and architecture simple, but it does not identify the risk that prolonged post-training could invalidate constraints imposed by the architecture’s design goals.

sol-6.1.text:
I think simplicity gives us a clearer signal about what actually works. If we change the training objective, add several architectural components, and improve the result, it becomes difficult to understand where the improvement came from. A simple setup makes it easier to identify the bottleneck and learn something useful from each experiment.

That matters especially in pretraining, because every decision has to work at scale. Extra complexity needs to justify its cost in training efficiency, stability, and implementation. I would start with a simple objective and architecture, understand their limitations, and add complexity when there is clear evidence that it solves a real problem.
